source.title: The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling
source.summary: Tool use transforms LLMs into agents that act beyond their training data, and for code-capable models, programmatic tool calling extends this further by replacing rigid JSON calls with scripts that chain and parallelize naturally. However, a systematic evaluation of tools as code on an established benchmark across current and prior model generations under real-world task conditions has not been conducted. In this work, we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4. In the programmatic tool calling paradigm, tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn. Programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement over the JSON tool calling baseline. Further, it matches or outperforms baseline in 13 of 14 models under parallel fan-out, and holds stable under context rot conditions where baseline degrades 2.3% on average. Our results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance tracking model capability across release generations.

previous_facts.evaluation_context: 309-entry BFCL v4 subset across 8 task categories (simple_python, multiple, parallel, parallel_multiple, live_simple, live_multiple, live_parallel, live_parallel_multiple). 14 models evaluated spanning Anthropic (5 models) and OpenAI (9 models) from November 2024 to July 2026. All experiments at temperature 0. Ablation studies: chaining (n=52, chain lengths 2-20), parallelism (n=32 enumeration entries, fan-out 7-48 plus probes), context rot (n=31 per condition). Deterministic scorer with normalized string comparison. 95% Wilson confidence intervals reported.
previous_facts.limitations: Results divide along model generation lines: all Anthropic models and three newest GPT generations match/exceed baseline, while three older GPT models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.4-mini) do not. Small ablation sample sizes (n=31-52) produce wide confidence intervals; only cross-model aggregate patterns treated as reliable. Evaluation limited to representative BFCL v4 subset, not full benchmark. No evidence presented on end-to-end task latency or token consumption—only accuracy metrics reported. Production deployment costs and error recovery not evaluated.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to Agent工具执行链优化. Programmatic tool calling addresses the topic's core question about whether tool calling parallelization introduces correctness risks by demonstrating it matches or exceeds JSON baseline in 13/14 models under fan-out conditions. However, the paper does not report Read/Grep/tool call counts, token consumption, or end-to-end latency—key metrics in the project context. The mechanism (single-turn code execution vs multi-turn JSON calls) may reduce redundant reads and context-building overhead in code agents, but this is not empirically measured in the visible evidence.
